title: What a large language model is

sections.skill: Describe what a large language model does

questions.prompt: What is the core job a large language model is trained to do?

choices.text: Store a copy of the internet to read from
Predict a likely next piece of text
Look up each answer in a database of verified facts
Follow a fixed rule list written by programmers

questions.correct_answer: Predict a likely next piece of text
questions.intro: A LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL (LLM) is a model trained on enormous amounts of text to do one core job: given some text, predict a likely next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, produces sentences, answers, stories or code. Because it learned from so much writing, an LLM can imitate many styles and often produces useful, relevant text. But predicting likely text is not the same as looking up facts or reasoning like a person. An LLM has no built-in way to check truth, so its output can be plausible and wrong. "Large" refers to the size of the model and its training data.
questions.feedback: An LLM predicts likely next text, repeatedly.

sections.skill: Compare an LLM with a phone's word suggestions

questions.prompt: After "See you," why might a phone suggest "soon"?

choices.text: It knows when you will meet
"Soon" often comes next in messages
It was told by your friend
It checked your calendar for the date

questions.correct_answer: "Soon" often comes next in messages
questions.intro: When you type a message, your phone may suggest the next word: after "See you," it might offer "soon" or "tomorrow." It suggests words that often come next, not words it has checked are true for you. A large language model works on a similar core idea at a far bigger scale. It was trained on huge amounts of text, so it can continue whole sentences and paragraphs in many styles. The scale makes it much more capable than a phone keyboard, but the basic job is still predicting likely text.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Avoid both extreme claims about LLMs

questions.prompt: A friend says, "LLMs are just autocomplete, so they are useless." What is the best response?

choices.text: Correct; they cannot help with any real task
Correct; autocomplete never produces sentences
Wrong; LLMs never predict text at all
Prediction at large scale can still be very useful

questions.correct_answer: Prediction at large scale can still be very useful
questions.intro: People sometimes describe LLMs with extreme claims: "it is just autocomplete, so it can do nothing useful," or "it knows everything, so it is always right." Both mislead. Predicting text well, at large scale, produces abilities that are genuinely useful, such as drafting, summarizing and explaining. Yet the same process can produce confident errors, because a likely-sounding sentence and a true sentence are not always the same. Judge an LLM by testing it on your task and checking facts, not by a slogan about what it "really" is.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, "It knows everything, so I never check it." What is the risk?
